title: Chapter 7: Speak His Name Into the Mic
content: The jacket is too big in the shoulders. It smells of diesel and wet rope and something older, tobacco gone cold in the lining, and Wren has not washed it, because washing it would be the end of that.

Ridge Road climbs the bluff in two turns. From the second turn she can see the tent: white canvas, six strings of bulbs, cars parked nose to tail on the lawn with their engines off and their hoods ticking.
She has never been inside Kestrel House. She has seen the roof from the water for twenty-four years, long and gray above the trees, and she has never once had a reason to walk up the hill.
Tonight the reason is printed on a card in her pocket. The Riverfront Revival. Six o'clock. Hosted by the Basin Authority, District 4. Proceeds to benefit the Kestrel Bend Promenade Fund.
There is a girl at the door with a clipboard and a smile she has been taught at some seminar in Columbus.
"Name?"
"Wren Aubrey."
The pen stops. The girl runs it down the list once, then again, the way people check a word they are certain they have spelled right.
"I don't have you."
"I know."
"You're not on the list."
"I'm not on the list," Wren says, and walks past her.

Inside, the tent is warmer than the house would be. Round tables, white cloths, a bar with two men in vests. On a trestle table near the front there is a model of the riverfront under a glass case, maybe four feet long, built by somebody patient. The ferry landing is gone from it. In its place is a boardwalk with railings and lamps and benches, and a little painted sign that says MILE 9 PROMENADE, and where the ferry should be there is open water, clean and empty and blue.
She stands over it long enough that a woman in pearls asks if she is all right.
"Yes," Wren says. "I'm looking at the water."

Ottoline Reeve is at the front of the tent in a gray dress, her hair done in a way that would survive a wind. She is not working the room. She is letting the room come to her, and the room is coming, one couple at a time, and each one laughs at something she says quietly.

Celia is by the bar in pale green, holding a glass she has not drunk from. Theo is beside her in a jacket that fits him better than the one he wore two summers ago, and his hand is on the small of Celia's back in the way of a man who has practiced it.

He sees Wren. His face does the thing she remembers, the small drop at the mouth, the eyes going somewhere else and coming back. Celia follows his look, and her face does something too, quicker and better hidden, and she moves her shoulder so that his hand has to stay where it is.
"Ladies and gentlemen." Ottoline has not raised her voice. The tent quiets anyway. "Thank you for coming up the hill."
She stands with one hand on the podium and does not use a note.

"The ferry at Mile 9 was built in 1908. It has crossed this river, in fair weather and foul, for one hundred and eighteen years. My grandfather rode it. Many of yours did. I want to say plainly that this Authority respects that history, because what I am about to describe will be described by others as an ending, and it is not."
She lets that sit.

"What it is, is a replacement. The ferry is an asset at the end of its service life. The cable is original to 1961. The hull was patched in 1988 and again in 2004. We have run the numbers, and the numbers are not sentimental."
A man at the back laughs. Nobody joins him.

"The promenade will be eleven hundred feet of public boardwalk, with lighting, a launch ramp, benches, and a river walk that connects the east bank to Mill Street for the first time in this town's history. It will not close at nine. It will not need a ferryman. It will be there at two in the morning, for anyone."
She lifts her chin slightly.
"A river is a machine. We do not ask a machine to be sorry. We maintain it."
The applause is real. It goes on longer than Wren expects. Celia claps with her fingers spread, watching the room instead of her mother.

Wren goes to the bar because her mouth is dry and because standing still in a tent full of strangers is a thing she has not practiced. The bartender asks what she wants. She says water. He gives her a glass with a lemon wedge in it, which feels like an insult she cannot explain.
"You're the ferry," Celia says, at her shoulder.
"I'm not the ferry."

"You know what I mean." Celia's glass is still full. Up close her eyes are tired and her dress is expensive and there is a small, real crack in her voice when she says, "I'm sorry about your grandfather."
"Thank you."
"My uncle drowned." She says it fast, and then looks surprised at herself, and then corrects the sentence the way a person straightens a picture. "In a boating accident. A long time ago."
Wren waits. People who say a thing fast usually want to say it again.
"I don't remember him," Celia says. "I was one." She lifts her chin toward the front of the tent. "She doesn't like it when I bring him up."
The bartender moves away with his towel.
"Why are you telling me?"
"I don't know," Celia says, and then, with a smile that arrives too late to be real, "Enjoy the auction."

The auctioneer takes the podium in a bow tie with a tiny brass gavel, and he is good at this, warm and quick, and he starts the bidding on item fourteen, a watercolor of the promenade donated by the architect, framed, five hundred dollars to start.
"Five hundred, thank you, sir. Six? Six hundred in the back. Seven?"
Wren walks up the center aisle.

She is aware of her boots on the canvas floor, which is not a floor but a mat, and of the chairs turning, one after another, a sound like cards being dealt. She is aware of the jacket, which hangs past her wrists, and of her hands inside the sleeves.
The auctioneer sees her coming and does not stop, because men like him do not stop, and that is the last mistake he makes all night.

She takes the microphone out of his hand. It comes easily. He is still holding the pose of a man holding a microphone, fingers curved around nothing, and the gavel is in his other hand and he does not use it.
The speakers pop. The tent goes quiet the way a room goes quiet when a glass is about to fall.
"Elias Aubrey," she says.
Her voice comes back at her from the trees, delayed and flat.

"He ferried this crossing for fifty-one years. He started in 1975, when he was twenty-seven, and he stopped on Saturday the twelfth of September, at nine forty-seven at night, when the gate opened upstream and the water came up six feet in ninety seconds and took him off his own deck."
Nobody moves.
"He drowned," she says. "That's the word. Drowned. I pulled him out of the river myself and he drowned, and nobody in this county will write it down."

She counts the silence. She has counted everything for ten days, hours in a lobby, stamps on other people's paper, and she counts this too. One. Two. A woman's bracelet ticks against a glass. Three. Four. The auctioneer lowers his hand. Five. Six. A chair leg finds the seam in the mat. Seven. Eight. Somewhere behind the tent a car door closes, and the sound arrives whole, and nobody in the tent turns to it. Nine. Ten.
Eleven.
"Thank you, Miss Aubrey," Ottoline says. Her voice is exactly as warm as it was at the podium. "That will be all."

The security man is at Wren's elbow before she has lowered the microphone. He is maybe fifty, with a mustache and a jacket cut to hide a radio, and he does not grab her. He puts his hand under her elbow, the way you would help a person across ice.
"Ma'am," he says. "I'll walk you out."
"I can walk."
"I know you can. I'll walk you anyway."

He does. Down the aisle, past the tables, past the model with its clean blue water, and the room watches her go and says nothing, and that is the part she will remember, not the eleven seconds, but the sixty after it, four hundred people holding their forks.
The girl with the clipboard holds the tent flap open. Her eyes are wet and she will not look up.
Outside, the gravel is loud. The air off the river is ten degrees cooler than the tent, and she stands in it and breathes until her hands stop.
"Miss."

He is young, twenty-five or so, with a camera on a strap and a lanyard that says KESTREL COUNTY LEDGER, and he has been standing at the edge of the bulbs for a while, judging by the dew on his shoulders.
"I'm sorry," he says. "I'm not with them. I'm with the paper. I've been covering this thing for three weeks and I've written the word promenade about four hundred times."
Wren looks at the camera.
"Did you get a picture?"
"I got one through the flap. You with the mic. It's mostly your back." He hesitates. "It's a good back."
She almost laughs. It would be the first time in ten days and she does not want to spend it here.
"What do you want?"
"Your name," he says. "Spelled right. I've been calling you the ferryman's granddaughter in my notes and that's not a name."

She looks down the hill. Below the bluff the river is black and the gate lights are three red dots at Mile 12, and the ferry is a shape at the landing with its lights off, waiting for morning. There is a brass clock screwed to the wheelhouse wall that runs four minutes fast, and she has not fixed it, and she is not going to.
"Wren Aubrey," she says.
"Wren like the bird?"
"Like the bird."
He writes it in a notebook with a pen he has to shake. He writes it slowly, the way people write when they intend to print it.

Nobody in Kestrel Bend has written anything down for ten days. She watches his hand move and thinks, with a flat and total clarity, that this is the first time since the twelfth of September that her family's name has gone onto paper without a stamp refusing it.
"One more thing," he says. "If I put this on the front page, is there anything you want people to know?"
Wren pulls the jacket tighter. It still smells like him. It will smell like him for a while yet.
"Tell them the water came up six feet," she says, "and there was no siren."
highlight: Wearing Elias's jacket, Wren takes the microphone at the Revival and says his name and the time.
